newsitem.title: UK: British police triumph dims IRA truce hopes.
newsitem.headline: British police triumph dims IRA truce hopes.

text.p: British anti-terrorist squads have scored a major victory against one of Europe's most persistent guerrilla organisations by seizing enough IRA explosives to devastate several city centres.

One Irish Republican Army suspect was shot dead and five others arrested in Monday's dawn raids which dealt a hefty blow to the morale of the guerrillas battling for Irish unity and dimmed hopes for an early ceasefire.
British police believe the IRA were within hours of launching lorry bomb attacks and targeting high-profile public figures with booby-trapped car bombs.
Security experts now believe the IRA could strike back to show it still has muscle.
Prime Minister John Major, delighted by the find but swift to condemn the IRA, phoned his Irish counterpart John Bruton on Monday night to give him details of the police swoop.
The biggest casualty could be the already fragile peace process in Northern Ireland where Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, has been excluded from all-party talks.

Major, who has invested much political capital in finding a solution to one of the 20th century's most intractable conflicts, said: "It remains impossible to reconcile Sinn Fein's rhetoric with the IRA's preparations for murder."
Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams blamed Britain for creating such a dangerous political vacuum.
He virtually conceded that the chance of a renewed IRA truce had evaporated. "This incident underlines the seriousness of the situation," a grim-faced Adams told reporters in Belfast.

The IRA ended a 17-month ceasefire in February with an attack on London's Docklands district that killed two people. In June, a huge lorry bomb devasted the centre of Manchester, injuring 200 people in the northern English city.
The pattern looked set to be repeated with devastating effect and British police believe they pounced just in time.
They seized 10 tonnes of home-made explosives and two pounds of Semtex explosive along with Kalashnikov rifles, timer devices, booby trap bombs and lorries ready for use in attacks.
All are favourite guerrilla weapons of the IRA in its 25-year battle to oust Britain from Northern Ireland.
One suspect was shot dead. Among the five arrested was a British Airways engineer seized at London's Gatwick Airport.
The airline confirmed the man's arrest but a spokesman insisted: "There is no indication to suggest that today's police operation has any connection whatsoever with air travel."

Police and secret service agents co-operated closely in a surveillance operation which had lasted for several weeks. Police chiefs said an IRA attack on the British mainland had been imminent, possibly within 24 hours.
